headline: Sound shore bass turn on as water hits 68 — Plum Gut pushing bait west
subhead: Schoolies thick from Mattituck to Rocky Point as thermal break stacks bunker on the flood.
body_markdown:
Water hit 68 degrees this week and the Sound shore woke up. Been fishing these beaches sixty years and I can tell you — when that thermometer climbs past 67, the bass start moving serious. Saw it happen Tuesday morning, dead calm conditions with light northwest wind, and suddenly the schoolies were everywhere from Mattituck Inlet clear east to Rocky Point.

The action's been best on the flood tide, first two hours after the turn. Water's been clean, that pale green you want to see, and the bait's stacked thick along the drop-off. Mostly peanut bunker with some spearing mixed in. Bass are feeding aggressive — not the lazy spring picking we had in May. These fish want to eat.

Best fishing's been bucktails with white Gulp Swimming Mullets, 3/4-ounce heads in the 15 to 25-foot range. Drag them slow on the drift, let the current do the work. Had good luck with chartreuse too when the water's got a little color to it. The key's been staying mobile — fish a spot for twenty minutes, if nothing's happening, move on. They're schooled up but they're moving.

Horton Point's been producing steady bass in the 24 to 30-inch range. Nothing huge, but good action if you time it right. The rocky structure there holds bait on the slack water, and when the current picks up, the bass move in to feed. Been using fishfinder rigs with fresh bunker chunks, 3/0 circle hooks, fishing right on the bottom. The bite's been best hour before peak flood.

Plum Gut's been interesting this week. The Race is running hard with these spring tides — we're coming off the new moon — and it's pushing a lot of bait west into the Sound. Been seeing good marks on the fish finder along the Orient Point approach, but you need to know that water. Current runs six knots on the peak, and if you're not positioned right, you'll spend more time fighting the drift than fishing.

Porgy fishing's been solid too, especially around the oyster cages east of Rocky Point. Water's warm enough now that they're feeding regular. Small pieces of clam on high-low rigs, size 4 hooks, fish it on the anchor. Nothing fancy, but steady action. Seeing fish in the 12 to 14-inch range, good eating size.

Weakfish showed up this week for the first time since early May. Not thick, but they're around. Caught three Tuesday evening on small bucktails with pink Gulp, fishing the edges of the eelgrass beds on the outgoing tide. These are the early scouts — if the pattern holds, we should see more as the water warms another degree or two.

Bluefish have been scarce, which is fine by me. Rather have bass anyway. Saw a few small ones mixed in with the schoolies, but nothing worth targeting. They'll show up when they show up.

Looking ahead, we've got a full moon coming Friday, which means big tides all weekend. That's going to flush a lot of bait out of the bays and harbors, and the bass know it. I'm watching the inlet mouths at sunset — that's when the real action usually starts. Water temperature's climbing steady, should hit 70 by the weekend if this weather holds.

The northwest wind pattern we've had all week is breaking down. Forecast shows southwest winds picking up Thursday, which could dirty up the water some, but it might also push more bait inshore. Either way, the fish are here now, and they're feeding. Just need to be in the right place when the tide turns.
